The continents have all been spoken for. We have satellite imagery of the deepest trenches and thermal scans of the thickest jungles. If you want to see the shape of an island in the South Pacific, you do not hire an explorer; you tap a piece of glass in your pocket. The world, in its physical dimensions, has been thoroughly caught.

And so, Arthur became a cartographer of the ephemeral. 

His studio smelled of ozone, dried lavender, and old paper. It occupied the fourth floor of a building that leaned slightly to the west, as if tired of standing up straight. His drafting table was not covered in rulers and protractors, which are tools for stubborn, unyielding things like mountains and property lines. Instead, Arthur used instruments of his own devising: a pendulum made of sea glass, ink distilled from rainwater caught during an autumn equinox, and vellum thin enough to read through.

He did not map places. He mapped *whens* and *hows*. 

On the wall behind him hung some of his finest work. There was a topographical chart of the silence that falls over a dining room just after someone says something unforgivable—all jagged, freezing peaks and sudden, breathless abysses. Beside it was a delicate, sprawling diagram of the exact trajectory of a stray dog’s afternoon in Naples, traced in warm ochre and smelled faintly of roasted garlic. 

On a Tuesday that felt remarkably like a Thursday, a client arrived. 

She was an elderly woman named Clara, though she carried herself with the impatient posture of someone much younger, annoyed that her bones were no longer keeping pace with her mind. She sat in the velvet armchair opposite Arthur’s desk and placed a small, tarnished silver locket on the blotter. 

"I don't want what's inside mapped," she said, before Arthur could speak. "The photograph is gone anyway. Washed out in a flood in seventy-four. I want a map of the porch."

"Which porch?" Arthur asked, picking up a pencil with a lead made of compressed ash. 

"My grandmother’s," Clara said. "August, 1958. Specifically, the hour between five and six in the evening, just before supper, when the heat finally broke."

Arthur nodded slowly. Memory mapping was delicate work. The terrain was notoriously unstable; mountains of significance had a habit of eroding over the decades, while trivial molehills grew into towering monuments. 

"Tell me about the borders," Arthur said, pulling a fresh sheet of vellum toward him. "What kept this hour contained?"

Clara closed her eyes. "To the north, the screen door. It had a rusted spring that sang in C-sharp every time my cousin Billy kicked it open. That’s a hard border. Beyond that was the kitchen, which was too hot to enter. To the south, the hydrangea bushes—blue ones, the size of prizefighters. Beyond them was the dirt road, which might as well have been the edge of the earth."

Arthur’s pencil moved in soft, whispering strokes. He didn't draw a rectangle for a porch. He drew a crescent of shelter, shaded in the cool, dusty blue of hydrangeas. On the northern edge, he sketched a jagged, metallic coastline to represent the singing screen door—a boundary that was constantly being breached and snapping shut.

"And the climate?" Arthur asked. "The prevailing winds?"

"Still," she murmured, her fingers lightly tapping the arms of the chair. "Thick and yellow, like pond water. Until about five-thirty. Then the wind would come off the creek at the bottom of the hill. It smelled of wet mud and crushed mint. You could feel it hit your ankles first, under the rocking chair."

Arthur switched to a fine brush dipped in pale green watercolor. He painted currents swirling up from the bottom right corner of the page, sneaking beneath the foundational lines he had drawn. He added tiny, stippled eddies to show how the breeze got trapped in the hems of cotton skirts and around the sweating glass of a pitcher of iced tea. 

For two hours, they excavated the sixty-minute territory. 

Arthur mapped the Archipelago of the Radio—a series of floating, disconnected islands of sound drifting from a transistor sitting on the windowsill, playing tinny baseball commentary and static. He charted the Great Divide of the floorboards, where the sun hit the painted wood and made it too hot for bare feet, forcing the inhabitants to navigate a narrow, shaded strait near the house's siding. 

He asked her about the light, and she told him it was the color of bruised peaches. He asked her about the hazards, and she told him of the loose third step that had claimed the skin of her left knee, and the carpenter bees that hovered like tiny, rotundzeppelins near the eaves, harmless but terrifying. 

Slowly, the vellum filled. It looked nothing like a house. It looked like a living cell, or a weather system, or a constellation discovered in a teacup. It had latitude lines of boredom and longitude lines of anticipation. In the very center, where the gravity of the map was strongest, Arthur placed a tiny, compass-like rose. 

"What is that?" Clara asked, leaning forward, her eyes bright and wet as she looked at the drying ink. "Right there in the middle."

"That is the epicenter," Arthur said gently, setting his brush down in a jar of cloudy water. "Every map needs a point of reference. A True North. From what you’ve told me, the entire hour revolved around the moment your grandmother stopped peeling apples, looked out at the yard, and said, *‘Listen to the cicadas. Summer’s almost spent.’*"

Clara stared at the paper. She reached out a trembling finger, hovering just a millimeter above the pale green currents of creek-wind and the bruised-peach wash of the late sun. 

"You got the scale wrong," she whispered, though there was no anger in her voice. "The porch wasn't nearly this big. I went back ten years ago. It was just a cramped little slab of rotting pine."

"Architects measure with tape," Arthur replied, carefully rolling the dried vellum and tying it with a piece of twine. "I measure by capacity. A ten-foot porch that holds the entire world has to be drawn rather large, otherwise the borders will burst."

Clara took the scroll. She didn't ask the price; she simply left the tarnished silver locket on his blotter. Arthur didn't object. An empty locket was a prime piece of real estate—a tiny, silver room waiting to be mapped.

After her footsteps faded down the creaking stairs, Arthur turned back to his window. Outside, the city was doing its best to be permanent, all brick and steel and asphalt. A flock of starlings erupted from a telephone wire, twisting into a dark, chaotic ribbon against the gray sky before vanishing behind a water tower. 

Arthur reached for a fresh sheet of paper, dipped his pen in ink, and began to draw the shape of the sky where the birds had just been.
